name: Solomon Islands
prevalence_note: In 2025 the Central Bank, through the Solomon Islands Financial Intelligence Unit, described a money-mule pattern in which people are talked into sharing bank details and Visa debit cards so that cash can be hopped through several local accounts and collected overseas. The Bank has also warned of a Facebook profile impersonating the Governor, and the Royal Solomon Islands Police Force has warned of a Gmail address using the Commissioner's name to press people about court or police files.
cross_border_note: The country code is +677. CBSI says the mule chain typically ends with a Visa debit card that has been sent out of the country, so a Honiara-looking account or a sender who appears to be local still does not show that the payment is a lawful domestic transfer.

scams.name: Money-mule chain using local accounts and a Visa debit card sent overseas
scams.name_en: CBSI and SIFIU warning: social-media or phone approaches use fake jobs, aid, investments, romance or inheritance to capture bank details and hop deposits through several local accounts

red_flag_keywords.text: send your Visa debit card overseas
withdraw the deposit and pass it to another account
receive funds into your account for a fee
share your bank details for the inheritance

scams.signals_en: SIFIU/CBSI warn victims are lured on Facebook, WhatsApp or phone via fake jobs, grants, romance or inheritances to share bank details and hop cash/mobile transfers through local accounts until withdrawn abroad with a posted Visa debit.
scams.legit_en: CBSI warns never to give bank details or a Visa debit card to an online contact. Real Solomon Islands employers, banks or agencies never ask individuals to receive and forward unexplained deposits, which can be money laundering.
bait_tactics: Refuse to hand over a Visa debit card or account details to anyone introduced only on Facebook or WhatsApp.
Ask why cash would have to be taken out and then walked through several other local accounts if the payment were genuine.
Say the request will be put to the person's own bank, the Police, or SIFIU before any incoming deposit is accepted.

scams.name: Facebook profile impersonating the Central Bank Governor
scams.name_en: CBSI public notice 04/2025: a Facebook account uses the Governor's identity; the Bank says the Governor does not keep a personal official Facebook profile of that kind
context_keywords: Central Bank of Solomon Islands Facebook
message claiming to be from the Governor
request to add the official account

red_flag_keywords.text: add the Governor on a personal Facebook
the Governor asks you to transfer funds
private message from the Central Bank Governor

scams.signals_en: CBSI warned that a fake Facebook profile impersonating the sitting Governor is circulating. The Bank states the Governor does not maintain a personal official Facebook account with those photos and urges the public not to engage or add it.
scams.legit_en: Genuine CBSI communications use the Bank's website, official social pages or published office email—never a personal Facebook profile in the Governor's name. Report suspect accounts to CBSI or local authorities.
bait_tactics: Do not add or reply to a Facebook profile that claims to be the Governor; use only the Central Bank pages listed on cbsi.com.sb.
If the profile asks for money or personal details, say the matter will be raised with the Bank through its published office channel.
Ask a relative who received the same friend request to compare the page with the Bank's official site before responding.

scams.name: Gmail message pretending to be the Police Commissioner about a court file
scams.name_en: RSIPF warning: a Gmail account uses the Commissioner's name to demand an immediate response about a court or police file and may be a prelude to a money scheme
context_keywords: court decision on a case file

red_flag_keywords.text: reply at once about the court file
pay a fee to settle the police case
this Gmail is the Commissioner's office

scams.signals_en: The Royal Solomon Islands Police Force warned of a Gmail account using the Commissioner's name demanding an urgent reply on a court decision or case file. The Commissioner noted the address and signature are fake and may precede fraud.
scams.legit_en: A genuine RSIPF message does not arrive from an informal Gmail address in the Commissioner's name, and it does not demand money to influence a court or police file. The Force told the public to delete or ignore such mail.
bait_tactics: Leave the Gmail unanswered and say any real police question will be checked at a Police station or through a published RSIPF channel.
Point out that the signature or office address on the message does not match the Force's usual format.
Refuse to pay a fee or send account details in response to a threat about a case file.
